books.section: Topic 8.10 The African-American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)
The Civil Rights Movement in the 1960s: From Integration to Black Power

source: original; stimulus photograph viewed before writing

stimulus.source_note: Photograph: Malcolm X, New York World-Telegram and Sun photograph, public domain (copyright not renewed, via Wikimedia Commons). Account drawn from the grounding books (Barron's Ch. 10, Topic 8.10, "Malcolm X"; 5 Steps Ch. 27; Princeton Ch. 12, "Malcolm X"). The 1952-1964 dates, the April 1964 pilgrimage, and the February 21, 1965 assassination are in the books; the March 1964 break with the Nation of Islam, before the pilgrimage, is per the NYPL Malcolm X timeline.
stimulus.text: The photograph shows Malcolm X speaking into a microphone. Between 1952 and 1964 he was a leader of the Nation of Islam, a Black religious movement that taught Black people to organize among themselves and rely on their own efforts, separate from whites. Malcolm X urged Black people to claim their rights "by any means necessary" and rejected the goal of integration into white society. In March 1964 he left the Nation of Islam, and in April 1964 he made a pilgrimage to Mecca, where he saw Muslims of different races worshipping together as equals. On the pilgrimage he revised his views about separation, saying he could work with people of other races who sincerely opposed racism. On February 21, 1965, he was assassinated in New York by members of the Nation of Islam. His autobiography, published after his death, carried his ideas to a new generation of activists.

stem: Malcolm X's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1964 most directly changed his thinking in which way?

options.text: It convinced him to abandon politics and become a minister only
options.misconception: The passage says he kept working after the pilgrimage and said he could work with others against racism.

options.text: It led him to rethink separation and consider working across racial lines
It convinced him that integration was the only goal worth pursuing
options.misconception: The passage says he revised his views about separation, not that he adopted integration as his only goal.

options.text: It led him to rejoin the Nation of Islam as its leader
options.misconception: The passage says he had left the Nation of Islam before the pilgrimage, in March 1964.

rationales.A: The passage says after the pilgrimage he said he could work with people of other races who sincerely opposed racism.
rationales.B: The passage says that on the pilgrimage he saw Muslims of different races worshipping together as equals, and he revised his views about separation.
rationales.C: The passage says he revised his views about separation; it does not say he adopted integration as his only goal.
rationales.D: The passage says he had left the Nation of Islam before the pilgrimage, in March 1964.
rationales.general:
1. Before 1964 Malcolm X taught separation from whites.
2. On pilgrimage in Mecca he sees Muslims of different races worshipping together as equals.
3. He had already left the Nation of Islam in March 1964, before the trip.
4. He revises his views about separation and says he can work across racial lines.
Remember: A journey that changes what a person has seen can change what the person believes.
